text: Cassini's end-of-mission dive was designed to stop it accidentally impacting Enceladus, one of Saturn's moons that might host a subsurface ocean and even microbial life. The probe came from Earth, so it carries microbes that could contaminate the moon and make it harder to tell whether any detected chemistry was native. By deliberately crashing into Saturn, the mission control team could steer it away from the moon, keeping the orbit predictable until the final plunge. It's basically a planetary-protection move, not just to end the mission. The crash also stopped it from later drifting into another potentially habitable moon.

I bet that’s just your shoe dragging on the ground. When you ride, one leg is pushing or steering, and the other one is kind of just hanging out there. That stationary leg will scrape along the pavement if your foot isn’t lifted high enough. The friction on the sole is a lot of irritation for the skin and the shoe, and that constant rubbing really adds up over a long session. You can get a hot spot on the foot, or even a blister. Also, if your shoe sole is already worn down, it makes the dragging worse because there’s less material between the foot and the asphalt.

Honestly, the skin isn’t the only thing that’s bothering you. Your leg muscles have to stay tense to keep the foot up and in a fixed position, which leads to fatigue. If you’re trying to hold your leg out to the side while moving, your hip and ankle are working harder than you’d think. It’s like holding a weight out to your side while walking. The tension in the thigh and calf can build up fast, and that aches later.

The other big one is misalignment. If your foot is twisted or your knee is slightly bent, the whole leg is under uneven stress. Your ankle has to hold the foot in a fixed pose, and that’s a lot of strain on the joints. You might also be bracing for impact, which keeps the core and legs tight. If the pain is in the joint, check that your ankle isn’t twisting when you brake or turn. The constant drag will wear out the sole faster, which can change your balance a bit when you’re trying to keep the leg steady.

Try lifting that stationary foot a little higher, or keeping it bent more so the sole clears the ground. You can also relax the pushing leg less and let the other one do the work. I’ve seen a lot of skaters with this exact issue, and most of it comes down to how they hold their body while moving. Give your ankle a quick stretch and see if the pressure is gone.

Honestly, most of the small arms and light weapons come from the black market, and historically a lot of it has been smuggled across the borders from Iraq or Lebanon, or pulled from state arsenals. Why keep getting them? Because in a conflict where the front lines keep shifting, not having a gun basically means you're at the mercy of whoever's holding the ground. It's kind of like buying insurance when you're living through a war. They keep getting weapons as long as the fighting makes them feel unsafe, and that cycle just keeps going.

Hi Mark,

Honestly, that makes more sense than it sounds. A whole day of low-level movement, walking, carrying bags, standing, stopping, starting again, adds up into a kind of dull, all-over strain. It's not a headache, but your muscles and joints get fatigued in a way that doesn't show up immediately. That's your body saying it's been pushed past the point where things start to feel sore. If it keeps happening, stretching and short breaks help; otherwise, treat it as a signal rather than something mysterious. You're not imagining it either, and it's just your body's way of saying it's had enough.

Cheers,
Dan

Hey,
Thanks for writing about this. It sounds like a classic slip of the tongue. Your brother primed you with the repeated word silk, and that kind of verbal rehearsal can mess with nearby associations. Cows and milk are so strongly linked in your head that when he asked what cows drink, the answer milk popped out before the correct answer water did. It's basically the same thing as saying milk instead of water, even when you know better. I think your brain just grabbed the first available concept. It's not that you're confused about what cows drink; the repeated priming and the dairy association made milk the fastest response. If he wanted a real gotcha, maybe the silk repetition is a red herring, but I'd still call it an association error, not a deeper mental trap. Next time, just laugh it off, since it's a normal brain glitch.

Hey,

Good question, because the difference isn't really about cleaning power. A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner mostly adds surfactants and a little conditioning ingredient to one product, so it's basically shampoo with a bit of lather and slip. A 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner has to work on skin, hair and scalp, so the formula usually leans toward something that's mild enough for daily body use but still safe for hair. In practice that means a compromise: less aggressive cleansing than a dedicated shampoo, and usually not as much conditioning as a standalone conditioner. The big thing is that one product can't be optimized for everything, so if you have hair or skin issues, separate products often work better.

I've seen this a lot: the 3-in-1 is the most convenient, but you give up some performance. Also, the bodywash part usually has a lower concentration of cleansing agents than a true shampoo, which is why it won't make hair as squeaky clean. Honestly, if you want hair to feel soft without a separate rinse, a real conditioner is still the safer bet. The 3-in-1 is handy for travel, quick mornings, or kids, but it's not a magic replacement for all of them.

Hi Sam,

Good question. Basically, nobody measures the whole continent as one rigid block. What you're really after is how fast the tectonic plate under it is moving, and scientists measure that by tracking fixed ground stations. GPS and other satellite navigation systems can pin those stations to millimeter-level accuracy over time. If a marker shifts a couple centimeters per year, that's the rate. They also compare repeated surveys, and use relative positions across ocean basins. The tricky part is that a continent is not perfectly rigid; faults, subsidence and local deformation matter. So the answer depends on which station or region you're looking at. North America isn't moving as one smooth chunk. Also, some places use InSAR, a radar technique that watches ground movement from orbit. It's handy for spotting subsidence or uplift over wide areas. That's useful because continents can bulge, sink or slide along fault lines. So the fastest spot isn't always the average rate. I'm not sure every oceanic plate has the same exact rate. If you want, I can look up the specific plate you mean.

Cheers,
Alex

Yeah, the short answer is that inbreeding raises the chance of rare harmful genes showing up. IQ isn't one switch; it's shaped by a lot of genes working together. When people who are related have kids, they share a lot of the same ancestry, so both parents are more likely to carry the same rare variants. If a variant is recessive and harmful, it usually stays hidden in a single copy. But with inbreeding, those matching copies can end up together in the child, and the effect can show up.

You can think of it like this: if a harmful gene is like a missing piece, having just one copy is often okay. Having two copies means the child has no backup. Inbreeding doesn't create new bad genes; it increases the odds that the same inherited ones meet and get expressed. That's the basic science behind why offspring from related parents can have lower cognitive scores.

Honestly, the main reason an arm injury feels less intense is that the arm has fewer and less densely packed sensory nerves than many other parts of the body. Your chest, feet, or face have way more nerve endings, so they send stronger signals to your brain. Plus, the arm has a good mix of muscle, fat, and bone that soaks up impact. When something hits your arm, that padding helps reduce how sharp the pain feels. It’s not that the injury isn’t real—it is—but the combination of tissue type and nerve density means your brain registers it as milder. So if you’ve ever been hit in the arm and it didn’t hurt as bad as a hit to your knee or ribs, it’s mostly down to how your nerves and tissues are set up.

Think of your blood as a delivery network. Oxygen rides in hemoglobin, and carbon monoxide hijacks that network. CO binds to hemoglobin around 200 times more strongly than oxygen does, so when CO levels are high it can sit in the same spots oxygen should be using. That means oxygen can't get picked up or delivered to tissues. Your body still needs oxygen, but the blood is blocked. It's a silent problem, because CO has no color or smell, so you might not notice anything until you're already in trouble. CO2 is different. It's a normal waste gas that your lungs constantly remove, and at everyday indoor levels it's not something that blocks oxygen transport. It dissolves in the blood and is exhaled, rather than grabbing hemoglobin the way CO does. That's the main difference: CO steals the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin, while CO2 is part of normal gas exchange.

That doesn't mean CO2 is harmless in every situation. In very high concentrations, it can make the blood more acidic and disturb breathing. But for a new colleague, the practical point is this: in a normal building or office, CO2 buildup is an air quality issue, not the same kind of immediate oxygen-transport emergency that CO creates. CO is the one that can quietly prevent oxygen from reaching your organs, which is why it's so dangerous to breathe in confined or poorly ventilated spaces.

In practice, you're usually meeting CO when something is burning, like fuel, gas appliances or vehicle exhaust. Those are incomplete combustion sources. If ventilation is poor, CO can accumulate without you noticing. That's why detectors exist. CO2 is mostly your own breath and other occupants' breath. In a sealed room with many people, it can rise, but that's more about stuffy air and drowsiness, not oxygen transport being stolen.

You're not wrong to ask that, but the premise is a bit misleading. Some businesses did predate the industrial era, but they were usually local workshops, trade guilds, or family-run ventures. They weren't the kind of global brands you'd recognize from shops or ads today.

What changed was industrialization. Mass production, standardized goods, and wider distribution made it possible for companies to be famous across large regions. Older firms often didn't have that scale, and records of their names and operations were patchy. So it's not that pre-industrial businesses didn't exist, but that the conditions for broad, recognizable brand recognition really took hold later.

For a long time, pot was basically illegal almost everywhere in the US, and the only way around that was medical marijuana programs, which had their own limits. Today, a lot of states have legalized it, but not all of them (some are still strictly no). What bugs me is the patchwork you're stuck with: you can legally buy it in 30+ states, yet cross into a dry state and you're technically in trouble. In my experience, people get tripped up by that every time. I think full national legalization would fix most of it, and I'm pretty sure that's the direction we're moving in.

Short version: it's a tiny pump-and-leak system, not a battery. My body makes electricity by moving ions like sodium and potassium in and out of cells through channels. When a nerve or muscle cell fires, those channels open, sodium floods in, and the inside of the cell flips from negative to positive in a flash. That voltage swing travels along the cell, like a ripple down a row of dominoes. In the heart, this same trick runs at a steady rhythm (60 to 100 bpm). That's what the beep on a monitor is listening for. I've seen that beep a lot in hospital rooms.

I used to think a headache meant something was literally breaking inside my skull. It doesn’t. The pain is your nervous system reacting to what’s going on in the head, neck, and sinuses. For me, the tell is usually a dull pressure behind the eyes and a tight band around the temples after too much screen time. Dehydration, poor sleep, and clenching my jaw make it worse. My position is that the head hurts because irritation or inflammation is making the nerves and blood vessels in the scalp and face feel stretched. It’s less like a broken bone and more like a car’s warning light: the signal is there because something upstream needs attention. If I take a walk, drink water, and stop squeezing my teeth, it often eases. That’s why I treat headaches as a cue, not a curse. I’ve learned to check these small things first, because my headaches usually respond to the basics.

I can’t even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. We chose this place specifically because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it’d be easy. We put our names on their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn’t completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

So I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and there wasn't a line, which honestly threw me. The bill for 2 people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. I'd assumed it'd be in the same ballpark as a steakhouse, but after I left, I learned it actually costed a bit more than I'd expected to pay there.

I was kind of disappointed there was no steak. At that price I figured they'd offer at least some steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but I've seen those at other Las Vegas buffets for way less.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Crab legs you can get at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I'd never come across rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were new to me. The issue was no crab-claw crackers. Staff said there were wooden mallets, but our table was packed right next to the one beside us, so I didn't want to start cracking shells and send pieces flying at those people. So I just went with the crab legs.

The Asian station wasn't that distinctive either. It felt a lot like the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, though I didn't try any.

I'd call this buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what you get. If you're curious, it's worth a try once, especially if there's no wait. If the line's long though, I'd probably think twice.

I'm keeping it (4 stars) because the switches are good. The spacebar rattles. If you hit it with the edge of your thumb it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also glitches occasionally, so I get "eexample" and have to backspace. That happens about once a day, usually when I'm typing fast and not looking. I paid $38 and kept it for the switches. I asked the seller what they were, but the answer took a week. By then I'd already pried off a keycap and figured it out myself: brown tactiles, with a little bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. Compared to those, my old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard. I'm mostly on email for my job, often 2 to 3 hours at a stretch, and my wrists don't hurt by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Returning it would mean paying for shipping and boxing it up, and I'd be without a keyboard in the meantime. So it's staying on the desk. I'm just pressing the spacebar a bit closer to the middle these days.
